## The Source

Anthropic Engineering blog post, "Effective harnesses for long-running agents" (published Nov 26, 2025, by Justin Young). It is not a single annotated trajectory but a write-up of failure patterns Anthropic observed during internal experiments, followed by the harness design they built to fix them. The agent under analysis is Claude (Opus 4.5) running on the Claude Agent SDK in a loop across multiple context windows.

## The Task

The agent was given a single high-level prompt — **"build a clone of claude.ai"** — and asked to build a production-quality web app. Because the project cannot fit in one context window, the agent had to work across many discrete sessions, each starting "with no memory of what came before." The Claude Agent SDK already had compaction available to manage context within a session.

## What the Agent Did and Where It Went Wrong

The post describes the baseline behavior — Opus 4.5 running in a loop with only the high-level prompt and compaction, before the harness fixes were added. Several distinct failure patterns emerged:

**1. Trying to one-shot the app (context exhaustion mid-implementation).**
Given the broad prompt, the agent "tended to try to do too much at once — essentially to attempt to one-shot the app." This often led to the model "running out of context in the middle of its implementation." The session would end leaving "a feature half-implemented and undocumented." Compaction did not rescue this, because it "doesn't always pass perfectly clear instructions to the next agent."

**2. The next session lost the thread.**
Because the prior session left work half-done and undocumented, the following agent "would then have to guess at what had happened, and spend substantial time trying to get the basic app working again" — re-deriving state rather than making forward progress.

**3. Declaring victory early.**
A second failure mode appeared "later in a project. After some features had already been built, a later agent instance would look around, see that progress had been made, and declare the job done" — even though the app was not actually complete.

**4. Marking features done without real testing.**
A further failure mode: "Claude's tendency to mark a feature as complete without proper testing." Absent explicit prompting, Claude "tended to make code changes, and even do testing with unit tests or curl commands against a development server, but would fail [to] recognize that the feature didn't work end-to-end." So features were marked complete while being broken from a user's perspective.

## Signals / Feedback Available

- **Compaction** was the only built-in bridge between sessions; the post reports it was insufficient and passed unclear handoff instructions.
- Within a session the agent had **unit tests and `curl` checks against a dev server** as feedback, but these passed even when the feature was broken end-to-end, giving a false "done" signal.

## The Fixes Applied (and a Residual Failure)

After observing these patterns, Anthropic added a harness:
- An **initializer agent** that sets up `init.sh`, a `claude-progress.txt` log, an initial git commit, and a comprehensive **JSON feature list** (over 200 features for the claude.ai clone, e.g., "a user can open a new chat, type in a query, press enter, and see an AI response"), all initially marked `"passes": false`. JSON was chosen because the model is "less likely to inappropriately change or overwrite JSON files compared to Markdown files," and agents were told it is "unacceptable to remove or edit tests."
- A **coding agent** that works one feature at a time, commits to git, updates the progress file, and starts each session by running `pwd`, reading git logs/progress files, picking the highest-priority unfinished feature, running `init.sh`, and running a basic end-to-end Puppeteer test before building anything new.
- **Browser automation (Puppeteer MCP)** to test as a human user would, which "dramatically improved performance."

**Residual failure that remained even with the fixes:** Claude "can't see browser-native alert modals through the Puppeteer MCP, and features relying on these modals tended to be buggier as a result" — a limitation of its vision plus the browser-automation tooling.

## Final Outcome

The post frames the baseline (high-level prompt + compaction loop) as falling "short of building a production-quality web app." With the two-part initializer/coding-agent harness, feature-list scaffolding, git/progress artifacts, and Puppeteer-based end-to-end testing, performance improved substantially — though bugs tied to invisible alert modals persisted. No single quantitative success/failure score for a specific run is reported; the article reports failure *patterns* and the design changes that mitigated them.
